title: Left Rotate by One
description:
Shift every element of the array one position to the left. The first element moves to the end.

**Input:** one line of space-separated integers.

**Output:** the rotated array, space-separated.

examples.explanation: 1 moves from the front to the back.

title: Union of Two Sorted Arrays
description:
Given two arrays that are each sorted in non-decreasing order, print every **distinct** value that appears in either one, in increasing order.

Merge them with two pointers and skip a value if it equals the last one you printed — no set needed.

**Input:** two lines, each a sorted list of space-separated integers.

**Output:** the union, space-separated, in increasing order.

examples.explanation: Every value from 1 to 6 appears somewhere.

title: Max Consecutive Ones
description:
The array contains only 0s and 1s. Print the length of the longest run of consecutive 1s.

**Input:** one line of space-separated 0s and 1s.

**Output:** the length of the longest run of 1s (0 if there are none).

examples.explanation: The last three 1s form the longest run.

title: Leaders in an Array
description:
An element is a **leader** if it is strictly greater than every element to its right. The last element is always a leader.

Scan from the right while tracking the maximum seen so far.

**Input:** one line of space-separated integers.

**Output:** the leaders in their original left-to-right order, space-separated.

examples.explanation: 17 beats everything after it, so do 5 and 2.
Equal is not strictly greater, so only the last 5 leads.

title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
description:
The array is unsorted. Find the length of the longest set of values that form a run of consecutive integers (like 4, 5, 6, 7). The values may appear anywhere in the array; duplicates count once.

Sorting takes `O(n log n)`. With a hash set you can do `O(n)`: only start counting from a value `x` whose `x − 1` is missing.

**Input:** one line of space-separated integers.

**Output:** the length of the longest consecutive run.

title: Rearrange by Sign
description:
The array has an equal number of positive and negative numbers (and no zeros). Rearrange it so signs alternate, **starting with a positive number**, while keeping the original relative order of the positives among themselves and of the negatives among themselves.

**Input:** one line of space-separated non-zero integers, half positive and half negative.

**Output:** the rearranged array, space-separated.

title: Pascal's Triangle
description:
Print the first `n` rows of Pascal's triangle. Each row starts and ends with 1, and every inner value is the sum of the two values above it.

**Input:** one integer `n`.

**Output:** `n` lines; line `i` (starting at 1) has the `i` values of that row, space-separated.

title: Spiral Matrix
description:
Print all elements of an `r × c` matrix in spiral order: go right along the top row, down the right column, left along the bottom row, up the left column, then repeat on the inner layer.

**Input:** the first line has `r` and `c`, followed by `r` lines of `c` integers.

**Output:** all `r·c` values in spiral order, space-separated.

examples.explanation: Right 1 2 3, down 6 9, left 8 7, up 4, then the centre 5.

title: Rotate Matrix 90 Degrees
description:
Rotate an `n × n` matrix 90 degrees **clockwise**.

You can do it in place: transpose the matrix (swap `m[i][j]` with `m[j][i]`), then reverse every row.

**Input:** the first line is `n n`, followed by `n` lines of `n` integers.

**Output:** the rotated matrix, one row per line, values space-separated.

examples.explanation: The left column 1 4 7 becomes the top row read bottom-up: 7 4 1.

title: Set Matrix Zeroes
description:
Wherever the matrix has a 0, set that cell's **entire row and column** to 0. Decide using the original zeros only — zeros you write don't spread further.

**Input:** the first line has `r` and `c`, followed by `r` lines of `c` integers.

**Output:** the resulting matrix, one row per line, values space-separated.

examples.explanation: The centre zero clears the middle row and column.

title: Next Permutation
description:
Rearrange the numbers into the **next lexicographically greater permutation**. If the array is already the largest permutation (non-increasing), wrap around to the smallest one (sorted ascending).

From the right, find the first index `i` with `a[i] < a[i+1]`, swap `a[i]` with the smallest larger value to its right, then reverse the suffix after `i`.

**Input:** one line of space-separated integers (duplicates allowed).

**Output:** the next permutation, space-separated.

title: Subarray Sum Equals K
description:
Count the contiguous, non-empty subarrays whose elements add up to exactly `k`. Elements can be negative.

Keep a running prefix sum and a hash map of how many times each prefix sum has appeared: a subarray ending here sums to `k` once for every earlier prefix equal to `sum − k`.

**Input:** the first line is the array; the second line is `k`.

**Output:** the number of subarrays with sum `k`.

title: Majority Element II
description:
Find every value that appears **more than ⌊n/3⌋ times**. There can be at most two such values.

A counter map works; the extended Boyer–Moore vote finds the two candidates in `O(1)` extra space, followed by a second pass to verify them.

**Input:** one line of space-separated integers.

**Output:** the qualifying values in increasing order, space-separated, or `none` if there are none.

title: 4Sum
description:
Find all **unique** quadruplets of values `[a, b, c, d]` from four different positions whose sum equals `target`.

Sort the array, fix the first two values with nested loops (skipping repeats), and find the last two with two pointers — `O(n³)`.

**Input:** the first line is the array; the second line is `target`.

**Output:** one quadruplet per line, values in non-decreasing order, lines sorted lexicographically (compare first values, then second, …). Print `none` if there are no quadruplets.

title: Maximum Product Subarray
description:
Find the contiguous, non-empty subarray with the largest product and print that product.

A negative number flips the biggest product into the smallest and vice versa, so track both the maximum and the minimum product of subarrays ending at each position.

**Input:** one line of space-separated integers.

**Output:** the maximum product.

examples.explanation: The best you can do is 0.

title: Count Inversions
description:
An **inversion** is a pair of positions `i < j` with `a[i] > a[j]`. Count the inversions in the array.

Checking every pair is `O(n²)`. During merge sort, whenever an element from the right half is placed before the remaining elements of the left half, it forms an inversion with each of them — that gives `O(n log n)`.

**Input:** one line of space-separated integers.

**Output:** the number of inversions.

title: Count Digits
description:
Given an integer `n`, print how many digits it has. The sign does not count as a digit.

**Input:** one integer `n`.

**Output:** the number of digits in `n`.

examples.explanation: The minus sign is ignored, leaving 7, 0, 8.

title: Reverse the Digits
description:
Reverse the digits of an integer `n` and print the result. Leading zeros disappear after reversing (`120` becomes `21`), and a negative number stays negative.

**Input:** one integer `n`.

**Output:** `n` with its digits reversed.

title: Armstrong Number
description:
A number with `k` digits is an **Armstrong number** if the sum of each digit raised to the power `k` equals the number itself. For example `153 = 1³ + 5³ + 3³`.

Print `true` if `n` is an Armstrong number, otherwise `false`.

**Input:** one non-negative integer `n`.

**Output:** `true` or `false`.

title: Print All Divisors
description:
Print every positive divisor of `n` in increasing order.

Checking every number up to `n` works, but you only need to check up to `√n`: divisors come in pairs `d` and `n / d`.

**Input:** one positive integer `n`.

**Output:** the divisors of `n`, space-separated, in increasing order.

title: Check Prime
description:
Print `true` if `n` is a prime number, otherwise `false`. A prime has exactly two divisors: 1 and itself. 0 and 1 are not prime.

**Input:** one integer `n`.

**Output:** `true` or `false`.

title: GCD and LCM
description:
Given two positive integers `a` and `b`, print their greatest common divisor and least common multiple.

Use the Euclidean algorithm: `gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b)`, and `lcm(a, b) = a / gcd(a, b) × b`.

**Input:** one line with `a` and `b`.

**Output:** `gcd lcm` on one line.

title: Primes up to N
description:
Print every prime number less than or equal to `n`, in increasing order. If there are none, print `none`.

Testing each number separately is slow for large `n`. The **Sieve of Eratosthenes** crosses out multiples of each prime instead, in `O(n log log n)`.

**Input:** one integer `n`.

**Output:** the primes up to `n`, space-separated, or `none`.

title: Power of a Number (mod)
description:
Compute `x` raised to the power `n`, modulo `1000000007`.

`n` can be as large as 10^18, so multiplying `n` times is too slow. Use **fast exponentiation**: square the base and halve the exponent, multiplying into the result whenever the current bit of `n` is 1. That's `O(log n)`.

**Input:** one line with `x` and `n`.

**Output:** `x^n mod 1000000007`.

title: Lower and Upper Bound
description:
Given a sorted array (it may contain duplicates) and a value `x`, find:

- the **lower bound**: the first index whose value is `>= x`, and
- the **upper bound**: the first index whose value is `> x`.

If no such index exists, use `n`, the length of the array.

**Input:** the sorted array on the first line, `x` on the second.

**Output:** the lower bound and the upper bound, separated by a space.

examples.explanation: The first 2 is at index 1; the first value above 2 (5) is at index 4.
Every value is smaller than 10, so both are n = 3.

title: Floor and Ceil in Sorted Array
description:
Given a sorted array and a value `x`, print:

- the **floor**: the largest value in the array that is `<= x`, and
- the **ceil**: the smallest value in the array that is `>= x`.

Print `-1` for whichever one doesn't exist.

**Input:** the sorted array on the first line, `x` on the second. All values are non-negative.

**Output:** the floor and the ceil, separated by a space.

examples.explanation: 4 is the largest value ≤ 5 and 7 the smallest ≥ 5.

title: First and Last Occurrence
description:
Given a sorted array and a target `x`, print the index of the **first** and **last** occurrence of `x`. If `x` isn't in the array, print `-1 -1`.

Aim for `O(log n)`: run two binary searches, one that keeps moving left after a match and one that keeps moving right.

**Input:** the sorted array on the first line, `x` on the second.

**Output:** the first and last index of `x`, separated by a space.

title: Count Occurrences in Sorted Array
description:
Given a **sorted** array and a value `x`, count how many times `x` appears.

A linear scan works, but the array is sorted: find the first and last position of `x` with binary search and subtract, for `O(log n)`.

**Input:** the sorted array on the first line, `x` on the second.

**Output:** how many times `x` appears (possibly 0).

title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
description:
An array of **distinct** integers was sorted in increasing order and then rotated at some unknown pivot, so `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]` might become `[4, 5, 1, 2, 3]`. It may also not be rotated at all. Find the smallest element in `O(log n)`.

Compare the middle element with the last one: if it's bigger, the minimum lies to the right of the middle.

**Input:** one line with the rotated array.

**Output:** the minimum value.

examples.explanation: The array was rotated after 7; the minimum is 0.
Not rotated, so the first element is the minimum.

title: Single Element in a Sorted Array
description:
In a sorted array, every value appears exactly **twice** except one value that appears once. Find that value in `O(log n)`.

Before the single element, each pair starts at an even index; after it, pairs start at odd indices. Binary search on which side of the break the middle falls.

**Input:** one line with the sorted array (its length is odd).

**Output:** the value that appears once.

title: Peak of a Mountain Array
description:
A **mountain array** strictly increases up to a single peak and then strictly decreases. The peak is never the first or last element. Find the index of the peak in `O(log n)`.

If `a[mid] < a[mid + 1]` you're still climbing, so the peak is to the right; otherwise it's at `mid` or to its left.

**Input:** one line with the mountain array.

**Output:** the index of the peak (0-based).
constraints: The array is a valid mountain

examples.explanation: 9 at index 3 is the highest point.

title: Integer Square Root
description:
Given a non-negative integer `n`, print `⌊√n⌋`, the largest integer whose square is at most `n`. Don't use a built-in square root.

Binary search over `0 … n` for the last value `m` with `m × m <= n`.

**Input:** one integer `n`.

**Output:** the integer square root of `n`.

title: Nth Root of a Number
description:
Given `n` and `m`, find the integer `x` with `x^n = m`. If no such integer exists, print `-1`.

Binary search `x` in `1 … m`. Compute `x^n` with integer arithmetic so precision isn't an issue.

**Input:** one line with `n` and `m`.

**Output:** the integer `n`-th root of `m`, or `-1`.

examples.explanation: 2⁴ = 16 and 3⁴ = 81, so 69 has no integer 4th root.

title: Koko Eating Bananas
description:
There are piles of bananas, and the guard returns in `h` hours. Each hour you pick one pile and eat up to `k` bananas from it. If the pile has fewer than `k`, you finish it and wait out the rest of that hour.

Find the **smallest** eating speed `k` that lets you finish every pile within `h` hours.

The hours needed only go down as `k` grows, so binary search on `k` between 1 and the largest pile.

**Input:** the pile sizes on the first line, `h` on the second.

**Output:** the minimum integer speed `k`.

examples.explanation: With one hour per pile, k must be the largest pile, 30.

title: Minimum Days to Make Bouquets
description:
A garden row has flowers where flower `i` blooms on day `bloom[i]`. A bouquet needs `k` **adjacent** bloomed flowers, and each flower can be used in only one bouquet. Find the minimum day by which you can make `m` bouquets, or print `-1` if it's impossible.

**Input:** the bloom days on the first line, then `m` and `k` on the second line.

**Output:** the minimum number of days, or `-1`.

examples.explanation: By day 12, flowers 0–2 and 5–7 have all bloomed.
Six flowers are needed but there are only five.

title: Smallest Divisor Within Threshold
description:
Pick a positive integer divisor `d`, divide every array element by it and round each result **up**. Find the smallest `d` for which the sum of these rounded results is at most `threshold`.

Bigger divisors only shrink the sum, so binary search `d` between 1 and the largest element.

**Input:** the array on the first line, `threshold` on the second.

**Output:** the smallest valid divisor.

examples.explanation: Only d = 44 brings every term down to 1.

title: Ship Packages Within D Days
description:
Packages must ship **in the given order**. Each day you load packages onto the ship until adding the next one would exceed its capacity. Find the minimum capacity that ships everything within `d` days.

The capacity is at least the heaviest package and at most the total weight. Binary search between those, simulating the days for each guess.

**Input:** the package weights on the first line, `d` on the second.

**Output:** the minimum ship capacity.

title: Kth Missing Positive Number
description:
Given a strictly increasing array of positive integers and a number `k`, find the `k`-th positive integer that is **missing** from the array.

At index `i`, exactly `a[i] - (i + 1)` numbers are missing before `a[i]`. Binary search for where that count reaches `k`.

**Input:** the array on the first line, `k` on the second.

**Output:** the `k`-th missing positive integer.

examples.explanation: Nothing is missing up to 4; the missing numbers are 5, 6, 7… so the 2nd is 6.

title: Aggressive Cows
description:
Stalls stand at the given positions along a line (in no particular order). Place `k` cows in distinct stalls so that the **minimum distance** between any two cows is as large as possible. Print that largest minimum distance.

For a candidate distance `g`, greedily place cows left to right whenever the gap is at least `g`. If `k` cows fit, try a bigger `g`.

**Input:** the stall positions on the first line, `k` on the second.

**Output:** the largest possible minimum distance.

examples.explanation: Cows at 0, 3, 7 and 10 are at least 3 apart.
Put them at the ends, 1 and 6.

title: Allocate Books
description:
Books are arranged in order, with the given page counts. Split them among `m` students so that each student gets a **contiguous** block of at least one book and every book goes to someone. Minimize the largest number of pages any one student reads.

Print that minimum, or `-1` if there are fewer books than students.

**Input:** the page counts on the first line, `m` on the second.

**Output:** the minimum possible maximum pages, or `-1`.

examples.explanation: Four students but only three books.

title: Search a 2D Matrix
description:
Each row of the matrix is sorted, and the first value of each row is greater than the last value of the row above it. Decide whether `x` is in the matrix in `O(log(r·c))`.

Read row by row, the matrix is one sorted list, so binary search on index `i` and look at cell `(i / c, i % c)`.

**Input:** `r c` on the first line, then `r` rows of `c` integers, then `x` on the last line.

**Output:** `true` if `x` is in the matrix, otherwise `false`.

examples.explanation: 13 would sit between 11 and 16 but isn't there.

title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
description:
Given two sorted arrays, find the median of all their elements combined. If the total count is even, the median is the average of the two middle values.

Merging works in `O(n + m)`. The `O(log(min(n, m)))` approach binary searches a cut in the smaller array so that the left halves of both arrays together hold exactly half the elements, and everything on the left is `<=` everything on the right.

**Input:** the first sorted array on line 1, the second on line 2. Both are non-empty.

**Output:** the median with exactly one decimal place (for example `2.0` or `2.5`).

title: Check the i-th Bit
description:
Is bit `i` of `n` set? Bits are numbered from the right starting at 0, so bit 0 is the ones place.

Shift `n` right by `i` and look at the lowest bit, or AND `n` with `1 << i`.

**Input:** one line with `n` and `i`.

**Output:** `true` if bit `i` is 1, otherwise `false`.

title: Set and Clear the i-th Bit
description:
Given `n` and a bit position `i` (0 = rightmost), print two numbers: `n` with bit `i` forced to 1, and `n` with bit `i` forced to 0.

Use OR with `1 << i` to set, and AND with the complement `~(1 << i)` to clear.

**Input:** one line with `n` and `i`.

**Output:** `set cleared` on one line.

title: Check Power of Two
description:
Print `true` if `n` is a power of two (1, 2, 4, 8, …), otherwise `false`.

A power of two has exactly one set bit, so `n & (n − 1)` is 0 for it — and only for it (when `n > 0`).

**Input:** one integer `n`.

**Output:** `true` or `false`.

title: Count Set Bits
description:
Count how many 1s appear in the binary form of `n`.

A neat trick: `n & (n − 1)` removes the lowest set bit, so repeat it until `n` is 0 and count the steps.

**Input:** one non-negative integer `n`.

**Output:** the number of set bits.

title: Minimum Bit Flips
description:
How many single-bit flips does it take to turn `a` into `b`? Each flip changes one bit from 0 to 1 or 1 to 0.

The bits that differ are exactly the set bits of `a XOR b`.

**Input:** one line with `a` and `b`.

**Output:** the minimum number of flips.

title: XOR from 1 to N
description:
Compute `1 XOR 2 XOR … XOR n` (0 when `n` is 0).

Looping works for small `n`, but `n` here can be huge. Write out the first few prefix XORs and you'll spot a pattern that repeats every 4 numbers.

**Input:** one integer `n`.

**Output:** the XOR of all integers from 1 to `n`.

title: XOR of a Range
description:
Compute `L XOR (L+1) XOR … XOR R`.

XOR cancels itself out: the XOR from L to R equals (XOR from 1 to R) XOR (XOR from 1 to L−1).

**Input:** one line with `L` and `R`.

**Output:** the XOR of every integer in `[L, R]`.

title: Counting Bits up to N
description:
For every integer `i` from 0 to `n`, count the set bits of `i`.

Reuse earlier answers: `i` has the same bits as `i >> 1` plus its own lowest bit.

**Input:** one integer `n`.

**Output:** `n + 1` space-separated counts, for `i = 0, 1, …, n`.

title: Two Numbers Appearing Once
description:
Every number in the array appears exactly twice, except two numbers that appear exactly once. Find those two.

XOR of the whole array is `a XOR b`. Any set bit in it is a bit where `a` and `b` differ — use it to split the array into two groups and XOR each group.

**Input:** one line of space-separated integers.

**Output:** the two numbers that appear once, smaller first.

title: Divide Without Multiplying
description:
Divide `a` by `b` **without** using multiplication, division or modulo, truncating toward zero (`7 / -2 = -3`). The result must fit in a signed 32-bit integer; if it's larger than `2147483647`, print `2147483647`.

Subtract the largest `b × 2^k` that still fits, again and again, using shifts.

**Input:** one line with `a` and `b`.

**Output:** the truncated quotient.

title: Search in a BST
description:
Find the node with value `x` in a binary search tree and print the subtree rooted at it. At each node, go left if `x` is smaller and right if it's larger, so you only walk one path from the root.

**Input:** line 1 is a binary search tree as space-separated level-order values, with `null` for a missing child (an empty tree is just `null`). All values are distinct; every node's left subtree holds smaller values and its right subtree larger ones. Line 2 is `x`.

**Output:** the subtree rooted at `x` as space-separated level-order values with `null` for missing children (trailing `null`s omitted), or `null` if `x` isn't in the tree.

examples.explanation: 2 is the left child of 4; its subtree is 2 with children 1 and 3.
5 would be left of 7, but that spot is empty.

title: Delete Node in a BST
description:

- If `key` isn't in the tree, the tree doesn't change.
- If the node has **no children**, remove it.
- If it has **one child**, that child takes the node's place.
- If it has **two children**, copy the smallest value of its right subtree (its inorder successor) into the node, then delete that successor from the right subtree using these same rules.

Inserting values one by one works in O(n²) for skewed trees. For O(n), build recursively with an upper bound: a value belongs to the current subtree only while it is below the bound.

**Input:** one line with the preorder values, space-separated.

**Output:** the tree as space-separated level-order values with `null` for missing children (trailing `null`s omitted).

examples.explanation: 8 is the root; 5 1 7 form its left subtree, 10 12 its right.
Each value is larger than the last: a right chain.

title: Recover a BST
description:
A binary search tree had the values of exactly **two** nodes swapped by mistake. Fix it without changing the tree's shape, and print the repaired tree.

In an inorder traversal of the broken tree, the sorted order is violated in one or two places; the swapped nodes are the first node of the first violation and the second node of the last one.

**Input:** the broken tree as space-separated level-order values, with `null` for a missing child. Values are distinct.

**Output:** the repaired tree in the same level-order format (trailing `null`s omitted).

examples.explanation: 1 and 3 were swapped: the root should be 3 with 1 below it.

title: Largest BST Subtree
description:
Given a binary tree (not necessarily a BST), find the largest **subtree** that is a valid binary search tree and print its number of nodes. A subtree is a node together with **all** of its descendants. Valid means every node's left subtree holds strictly smaller values and its right subtree strictly larger ones.

Solve it in one post-order pass: each node reports whether its subtree is a BST, along with its size and its minimum and maximum values.

**Input:** a binary tree as space-separated level-order values, with `null` for a missing child (an empty tree is just `null`).

**Output:** the size of the largest BST subtree (0 for an empty tree).

examples.explanation: The subtree at 5 (5, 1, 8) is a BST; 15 → 7 isn't.
The whole tree is a BST.

title: Frog Jump
description:
A frog sits on stone `0` and wants to reach the last stone. Stone `i` has height `h[i]`. From stone `i` it can jump to stone `i + 1` or stone `i + 2`, and a jump from `i` to `j` costs `|h[i] − h[j]|` energy.

Print the minimum total energy needed to reach the last stone.

**Input:** one line with the heights `h[0] … h[n−1]`.

**Output:** the minimum total energy.

title: Frog Jump with K Steps
description:
Same frog, longer legs. From stone `i` the frog can jump to any of the next `k` stones (`i + 1` up to `i + k`). A jump from `i` to `j` costs `|h[i] − h[j]|`.

Print the minimum total energy to get from stone `0` to the last stone.

**Input:** the heights on the first line, `k` on the second.

**Output:** the minimum total energy.

examples.explanation: With k = 1 every stone is visited: 10 + 10 = 20.

title: House Robber II
description:
Houses stand in a **circle**, and house `i` holds `a[i]` coins. You can't take from two adjacent houses — and because it's a circle, the first and last houses are adjacent too.

Print the most coins you can collect.

**Input:** one line with `a[0] … a[n−1]`.

**Output:** the maximum total.

examples.explanation: Houses 0 and 2 are neighbours in the circle, so the best is 3.

title: Unique Grid Paths
description:
A robot starts in the top-left cell of an `m × n` grid and wants to reach the bottom-right cell. It may only move **right** or **down**.

Print how many different paths it can take, modulo `1000000007`.

**Input:** one line with `m` and `n`.

**Output:** the number of paths modulo `1000000007`.

examples.explanation: 28 ways to arrange 2 downs and 6 rights.

title: Unique Paths with Obstacles
description:
A robot moves only **right** or **down** from the top-left to the bottom-right cell of a grid. Cells marked `1` are blocked; `0` cells are free. If the start or the finish is blocked there are no paths.

Print the number of paths that avoid every blocked cell, modulo `1000000007`.

**Input:** `r c` on the first line, then `r` lines of `c` space-separated values (`0` or `1`).

**Output:** the number of paths modulo `1000000007`.

examples.explanation: Go around the centre rock: over the top or along the bottom.

title: Minimum Path Sum
description:
Each cell of a grid holds a non-negative cost. Walk from the top-left to the bottom-right cell, moving only **right** or **down**, and add up the costs of every cell you step on (including the first and last).

Print the smallest possible total.

**Input:** `r c` on the first line, then `r` lines of `c` space-separated costs.

**Output:** the minimum path sum.

title: Triangle Minimum Path
description:
A triangle of numbers has `i + 1` values on row `i`. Start at the top and move down one row at a time; from position `j` you can step to position `j` or `j + 1` on the next row.

Print the minimum sum of a path from the top to the bottom row.

**Input:** `n` (the number of rows) on the first line, then row `i` with `i + 1` space-separated integers.

**Output:** the minimum path sum.

title: Minimum Falling Path Sum
description:
In an `n × n` matrix, a falling path picks one cell in every row, starting anywhere in the first row. From column `j` the next row's cell must be in column `j − 1`, `j` or `j + 1`.

Print the smallest possible sum of a falling path.

**Input:** `n` on the first line, then `n` lines of `n` space-separated integers.

**Output:** the minimum falling path sum.

title: Subset Sum Exists
description:
Given an array of positive integers and a `target`, decide whether some subset of the array (any selection of elements, each used at most once) adds up to exactly `target`. The empty subset adds up to `0`.

**Input:** the array on the first line, `target` on the second.

**Output:** `true` or `false`.

title: Partition Equal Subset Sum
description:
Can the array be split into two groups with exactly the same sum? Every element must go into one of the two groups.

**Input:** one line of positive integers.

**Output:** `true` or `false`.

title: Minimum Subset Sum Difference
description:
Split the array into two groups (either may be empty) so that the absolute difference between their sums is as small as possible. Every element goes into exactly one group.

**Input:** one line of non-negative integers.

**Output:** the minimum possible difference.

title: Count Subsets with Sum K
description:
Count the subsets of the array whose elements add up to exactly `k`. Subsets are chosen by **position**, so equal values at different positions count as different subsets (and a `0` can be included or not). When `k = 0` the empty subset counts.

Print the count modulo `1000000007`.

**Input:** the array on the first line, `k` on the second.

**Output:** the number of subsets modulo `1000000007`.

title: 0/1 Knapsack
description:
You have `n` items; item `i` weighs `w[i]` and is worth `v[i]`. Your bag holds at most `W` weight. Each item can be taken **at most once**.

Print the largest total value you can carry.

**Input:** weights on the first line, values on the second, capacity `W` on the third.

**Output:** the maximum total value.

examples.explanation: Only one item fits at a time; the weight-1 item is worth the most: 3.

title: Coin Change II
description:
Given coin denominations (unlimited supply of each) and an `amount`, count the number of **combinations** of coins that add up to the amount. Order doesn't matter: `1 + 2` and `2 + 1` are the same combination. An amount of `0` has exactly one combination (use no coins).

Print the count modulo `1000000007`.

**Input:** the distinct coin values on the first line, `amount` on the second.

**Output:** the number of combinations modulo `1000000007`.

title: Unbounded Knapsack
description:
Like the 0/1 knapsack, but you have an **unlimited** supply of every item. Item `i` weighs `w[i]` and is worth `v[i]`; the bag holds at most `W`.

Print the largest total value you can carry.

**Input:** weights on the first line, values on the second, capacity `W` on the third.

**Output:** the maximum total value.

examples.explanation: Two of weight 4 plus one of weight 2: 11 + 11 + 5 = 27.

title: Rod Cutting
description:
A rod of length `n` can be cut into pieces of whole lengths. A piece of length `i` sells for `price[i]` (the first value is the price of length 1, the second of length 2, and so on). You may also sell the rod uncut.

Print the maximum money you can make from a rod of length `n`, where `n` is the number of prices given.

**Input:** one line with `price[1] … price[n]`.

**Output:** the maximum revenue.

title: Longest Common Subsequence
description:
A **subsequence** keeps some characters of a string in their original order (not necessarily adjacent). Print the length of the longest subsequence that the two strings share.

**Input:** two lowercase strings, one per line.

**Output:** the length of their longest common subsequence.

title: Longest Common Substring
description:
A **substring** is a run of consecutive characters. Print the length of the longest substring that appears in both strings (0 if they share no character).

**Input:** two lowercase strings, one per line.

**Output:** the length of their longest common substring.

title: Longest Palindromic Subsequence
description:
Print the length of the longest subsequence of `s` that reads the same forwards and backwards. A subsequence keeps characters in order but may skip some.

**Input:** one lowercase string `s`.

**Output:** the length of its longest palindromic subsequence.

title: Minimum Insertions to Make Palindrome
description:
You may insert characters anywhere in `s`. Print the fewest insertions needed to turn `s` into a palindrome.

Hint: the characters you don't need to touch form the longest palindromic subsequence.

**Input:** one lowercase string `s`.

**Output:** the minimum number of insertions.

title: Edit Distance
description:
Turn string `a` into string `b` using three operations, each costing 1: **insert** a character, **delete** a character, or **replace** a character.

Print the minimum number of operations.

**Input:** two lowercase strings, one per line.

**Output:** the minimum number of edits.

title: Distinct Subsequences
description:
Count how many ways `t` appears as a subsequence of `s`: each way is a different set of positions in `s` that spells `t` in order.

Print the count modulo `1000000007`.

**Input:** `s` on the first line, `t` on the second (both lowercase).

**Output:** the number of ways modulo `1000000007`.

examples.explanation: Choose which two of the three b's to use: 3 ways.

title: Wildcard Matching
description:
Check whether a pattern matches a whole string. In the pattern, `?` matches exactly one character and `*` matches any sequence of characters (including none). Every other character matches only itself.

**Input:** the string on the first line (lowercase letters), the pattern on the second (lowercase letters, `?`, `*`).

**Output:** `true` if the pattern matches the entire string, otherwise `false`.

examples.explanation: No way to line up the final `?b`.

title: Stock Trading with Unlimited Transactions
description:
`p[i]` is a stock's price on day `i`. You may buy and sell as many times as you like, but you can hold at most one share at a time (sell before you buy again). Buying and selling on the same day is allowed but pointless.

Print the maximum profit.

**Input:** one line of daily prices.

**Output:** the maximum profit (0 if no trade helps).

title: Stock Trading with Two Transactions
description:
Daily prices are given. You may complete **at most two** transactions (a transaction is one buy followed later by one sell), holding at most one share at a time.

Print the maximum profit.

**Input:** one line of daily prices.

**Output:** the maximum profit.

title: Stock Trading with K Transactions
description:
Daily prices are given along with `k`. You may complete **at most `k`** transactions (buy then sell), holding at most one share at a time.

Print the maximum profit.

**Input:** daily prices on the first line, `k` on the second.

**Output:** the maximum profit.

title: Stock Trading with Cooldown
description:
Daily prices are given. Trade as many times as you like, holding at most one share, but after you **sell** you must wait one full day before buying again (a one-day cooldown).

Print the maximum profit.

**Input:** one line of daily prices.

**Output:** the maximum profit.

examples.explanation: Buy, sell, cool down, buy, sell: 3.

title: Stock Trading with Transaction Fee
description:
Daily prices are given along with a `fee` charged once for each completed transaction (buy then sell). Trade as often as you like, holding at most one share at a time.

Print the maximum profit after fees.

**Input:** daily prices on the first line, `fee` on the second.

**Output:** the maximum profit.

title: Number of Longest Increasing Subsequences
description:
Count how many **strictly increasing** subsequences have the maximum possible length. Subsequences are chosen by position, so equal values at different positions give different subsequences.

Print the count modulo `1000000007`.

**Input:** one line of integers.

**Output:** the number of longest increasing subsequences modulo `1000000007`.

examples.explanation: Each single element is a longest one: 5.

title: Matrix Chain Multiplication
description:
Matrix `i` has size `d[i−1] × d[i]`, so `n` matrices are described by `n + 1` dimensions. Multiplying an `x × y` matrix by a `y × z` matrix costs `x · y · z` scalar multiplications. The product's value doesn't depend on how you parenthesise, but the cost does.

Print the minimum total cost to multiply the whole chain (0 if there is only one matrix).

**Input:** one line with the dimensions `d[0] … d[n]`.

**Output:** the minimum number of scalar multiplications.

title: Burst Balloons
description:
Balloons in a row carry numbers. Bursting balloon `i` earns `left · a[i] · right`, where `left` and `right` are the numbers on its current neighbours (a missing neighbour counts as `1`). After a burst, the neighbours become adjacent.

Burst every balloon in the best order and print the maximum total coins.

Hint: think about which balloon you burst **last** inside a range.

**Input:** one line with the balloon numbers.

**Output:** the maximum coins.

title: Palindrome Partitioning Min Cuts
description:
Cut the string into pieces so that **every piece is a palindrome**. Print the minimum number of cuts needed (0 if the whole string is already a palindrome).

**Input:** one lowercase string `s`.

**Output:** the minimum number of cuts.

title: Maximal Square
description:
A grid holds `0`s and `1`s. Find the largest square made entirely of `1`s and print its **area**.

**Input:** `r c` on the first line, then `r` lines of `c` characters, each `0` or `1` (no spaces).

**Output:** the area of the largest all-ones square (0 if there are no ones).

title: Count Square Submatrices
description:
A grid holds `0`s and `1`s. Count every square submatrix (of any size) whose cells are all `1`.

**Input:** `r c` on the first line, then `r` lines of `c` characters, each `0` or `1` (no spaces).

**Output:** the number of all-ones squares.

examples.explanation: 10 of size 1, 4 of size 2, 1 of size 3: 15.

title: BFS Traversal of a Graph
description:
Breadth-first search explores a graph in rings: first the start node, then everything one edge away, then everything two edges away, and so on.

Run BFS on an **undirected** graph from node `s` and print the nodes in the order they are visited. Whenever a node's neighbours are added to the queue, add them in **increasing order**. Nodes that can't be reached from `s` are not printed.

**Input:** The first line has `n` and `m` — the number of nodes (numbered `0` to `n − 1`) and edges. Each of the next `m` lines has an edge `u v`. The last line has the start node `s`.

**Output:** the visited nodes in BFS order, space-separated.

examples.explanation: From 0 visit 1 and 2, then their neighbours 3 and 4.

title: DFS Traversal of a Graph
description:
Depth-first search follows one path as deep as it can before backing up to try the next branch.

Run a recursive DFS on an **undirected** graph from node `s`: visit a node, then recurse into each unvisited neighbour in **increasing order**. Print the nodes in the order they are first visited. Unreachable nodes are not printed.

**Input:** The first line has `n` and `m` — the number of nodes (numbered `0` to `n − 1`) and edges. Each of the next `m` lines has an edge `u v`. The last line has the start node `s`.

**Output:** the visited nodes in DFS order, space-separated.

title: Number of Provinces
description:
There are `n` cities. City `i` and city `j` are directly connected when `M[i][j] = 1`. Cities connected directly or through other cities form one **province**.

Given the connection matrix `M`, print the number of provinces.

**Input:** the first line has `n`. Each of the next `n` lines has `n` space-separated values `0` or `1`. The matrix is symmetric and `M[i][i] = 1`.

**Output:** the number of provinces.

examples.explanation: Cities 0 and 1 are one province; city 2 is alone.

title: Flood Fill
description:
An image is a grid of single-digit colors. Starting from pixel `(sr, sc)`, repaint it and every pixel connected to it **up, down, left or right** through pixels of the **same original color** with the new color `k`.

Print the image after the fill. If `k` equals the starting pixel's color, nothing changes.

**Input:** the first line has `r c`. Each of the next `r` lines has `c` digits with no spaces. The last line has `sr sc k`.

**Output:** the `r` rows of the filled image, digits with no spaces.

examples.explanation: Every 1 connected to the centre turns into 2; the bottom-right 1 is cut off.
New color equals the old one, so the image is unchanged.

title: Rotting Oranges
description:
Each cell of a grid is `0` (empty), `1` (fresh orange) or `2` (rotten orange). Every minute, each fresh orange that is directly up, down, left or right of a rotten orange becomes rotten.

Print the minimum number of minutes until no fresh orange is left, or `-1` if some fresh orange can never rot. If there are no fresh oranges at the start, the answer is `0`.

**Input:** the first line has `r c`. Each of the next `r` lines has `c` digits with no spaces.

**Output:** the number of minutes, or `-1`.

examples.explanation: The rot spreads from the top-left corner and reaches the last orange after 4 minutes.
The bottom-left orange is isolated, so it never rots.

title: Distance to Nearest Zero
description:
Given a grid of `0`s and `1`s, find for every cell the distance to the nearest `0`, moving one step up, down, left or right at a time. Cells that are `0` have distance `0`. The grid has at least one `0`.

Running a BFS from every cell is slow. Start one BFS from **all zeros at once** instead.

**Input:** the first line has `r c`. Each of the next `r` lines has `c` digits with no spaces.

**Output:** `r` lines, each with `c` space-separated distances.
constraints: the grid contains at least one 0

examples.explanation: The bottom-middle cell is 2 steps from the nearest 0.

title: Surrounded Regions
description:
A board is made of `X` and `O` cells. A group of `O`s connected up, down, left or right is **captured** if none of its cells lies on the border of the board. Captured groups are flipped to `X`.

Print the board after flipping every captured group.

Tip: instead of checking each group, start from the `O`s on the border and mark everything they reach — whatever is left unmarked gets captured.

**Input:** the first line has `r c`. Each of the next `r` lines has `c` characters (`X` or `O`) with no spaces.

**Output:** the `r` rows of the resulting board.

examples.explanation: The middle group is enclosed and flips; the bottom O touches the border and stays.
Every O is on the border.

title: Number of Enclaves
description:
In a grid, `1` is land and `0` is sea. From a land cell you can walk to an adjacent land cell (up, down, left, right), and you can walk off the grid from any land cell on the border.

Print the number of land cells from which it is **impossible** to walk off the grid.

**Input:** the first line has `r c`. Each of the next `r` lines has `c` digits with no spaces.

**Output:** the number of enclosed land cells.

examples.explanation: The three 1s in the middle are boxed in; the 1 on the left edge can walk off.
The column touches the top and bottom borders.

title: Detect Cycle in an Undirected Graph
description:
Print `true` if an **undirected** graph contains a cycle, otherwise `false`. The graph can be disconnected.

During a DFS or BFS, reaching an already-visited node that isn't the one you came from means you have found a cycle.

**Input:** The first line has `n` and `m` — the number of nodes (numbered `0` to `n − 1`) and edges. Each of the next `m` lines has an edge `u v`.

**Output:** `true` or `false`.

title: Is Graph Bipartite
description:
An **undirected** graph is bipartite if its nodes can be split into two groups so that every edge connects nodes from different groups — equivalently, if you can color each node with one of two colors so no edge joins two nodes of the same color.

Print `true` if the graph is bipartite, otherwise `false`. The graph can be disconnected.

**Input:** The first line has `n` and `m` — the number of nodes (numbered `0` to `n − 1`) and edges. Each of the next `m` lines has an edge `u v`.

**Output:** `true` or `false`.

examples.explanation: Color 0 and 2 one way, 1 and 3 the other.

title: Detect Cycle in a Directed Graph
description:
Print `true` if a **directed** graph contains a cycle (a path that leads from a node back to itself), otherwise `false`. A self-loop counts as a cycle.

One way: run Kahn's algorithm — repeatedly remove nodes with no incoming edges. If some nodes can never be removed, they sit on a cycle.

**Input:** The first line has `n` and `m` — the number of nodes (numbered `0` to `n − 1`) and edges. Each of the next `m` lines has an edge `u v` going from `u` to `v`.

**Output:** `true` or `false`.

examples.explanation: Two paths to 3 but no way back: no cycle.

title: Topological Sort
description:
A topological order of a **directed acyclic graph** lists every node so that each edge `u → v` has `u` before `v`.

Many orders can be valid, so print the **lexicographically smallest** one: whenever several nodes are ready (all their predecessors are placed), take the smallest. Kahn's algorithm with a min-heap does exactly this.

**Input:** The first line has `n` and `m` — the number of nodes (numbered `0` to `n − 1`) and edges. Each of the next `m` lines has an edge `u v` going from `u` to `v`. The graph has no cycles.

**Output:** the topological order, space-separated.

examples.explanation: 1, 2 and 3 must wait; 4 is the smallest node free at the start.
No edges: every order is valid, the smallest is 0 1 2.

title: Course Schedule
description:
There are `n` courses numbered `0` to `n − 1`. A prerequisite pair `a b` means you must finish course `b` before course `a`.

Print `true` if it is possible to finish every course, otherwise `false`. It's impossible exactly when the prerequisites form a cycle.

**Input:** the first line has `n` and `m` (the number of prerequisite pairs). Each of the next `m` lines has a pair `a b`.

**Output:** `true` or `false`.

examples.explanation: Each course needs the other first.

title: Shortest Path in an Unweighted Graph
description:
In an **undirected** graph where every edge has length 1, find the shortest distance from node `s` to every node. BFS finds these distances in `O(n + m)`.

**Input:** The first line has `n` and `m` — the number of nodes (numbered `0` to `n − 1`) and edges. Each of the next `m` lines has an edge `u v`. The last line has the source `s`.

**Output:** `n` space-separated distances, where the `i`-th is the distance from `s` to node `i`, or `-1` if `i` is unreachable.

title: Shortest Path in a Binary Maze
description:
A maze is a grid where `1` is an open cell and `0` is a wall. From an open cell you can step to an adjacent open cell up, down, left or right.

Print the minimum number of steps from `(sr, sc)` to `(tr, tc)`, or `-1` if the target can't be reached (including when the start or target is a wall).

**Input:** the first line has `r c`. Each of the next `r` lines has `c` digits with no spaces. The last line has `sr sc tr tc`.

**Output:** the minimum number of steps, or `-1`.

examples.explanation: Go down, then right along the middle row, then down: 5 steps.
The two open cells only touch diagonally.

title: Word Ladder Length
description:
You can turn a word into another by changing **one letter at a time**, and every word you pass through (including the final one) must be in the given word list. The starting word doesn't need to be in the list.

Print the number of words in the shortest such sequence from `begin` to `end`, counting both `begin` and `end`. Print `0` if no sequence exists. All words have the same length and use lowercase letters, and `begin` differs from `end`.

**Input:** the first line has `begin`, the second `end`, the third the number of words `k`, followed by `k` lines with one word each.

**Output:** the length of the shortest sequence, or `0`.

examples.input:
hit
cog
6
hot
dot
dog
lot
log
cog
examples.explanation: hit → hot → dot → dog → cog is 5 words.

examples.input:
hit
cog
5
hot
dot
dog
lot
log
examples.explanation: cog isn't in the list, so it can't be reached.

title: Dijkstra's Shortest Paths
description:
Find the shortest distance from node `s` to every node in a **directed** graph with non-negative edge weights.

Dijkstra's algorithm repeatedly takes the closest unfinished node from a min-heap and relaxes its outgoing edges, in `O((n + m) log n)`.

**Input:** The first line has `n` and `m` — the number of nodes (numbered `0` to `n − 1`) and edges. Each of the next `m` lines has an edge `u v w` going from `u` to `v` with weight `w`. The last line has the source `s`.

**Output:** `n` space-separated distances, where the `i`-th is the distance from `s` to node `i`, or `-1` if `i` is unreachable.

examples.explanation: 0 → 2 → 1 costs 3, cheaper than the direct edge of 4.
Edges only leave node 1, so nothing is reachable from 0.

title: Network Delay Time
description:
A signal starts at node `k` and travels along **directed** edges, each taking `w` time units. Print how long it takes until **every** node has received the signal, or `-1` if some node never receives it.

That's the largest shortest-path distance from `k`.

**Input:** The first line has `n` and `m` — the number of nodes (numbered `0` to `n − 1`) and edges. Each of the next `m` lines has an edge `u v w` going from `u` to `v` with travel time `w`. The last line has `k`.

**Output:** the time for all nodes to receive the signal, or `-1`.

examples.explanation: Node 3 is the last to hear the signal, after 2 units.
From node 1 the signal can't reach node 0.

title: Cheapest Flights Within K Stops
description:
Cities are connected by one-way flights with prices. Find the cheapest way to fly from `src` to `dst` with **at most `k` stops** in between (that is, at most `k + 1` flights). Print `-1` if there's no such route. Flying from a city to itself costs `0`.

Plain Dijkstra ignores the stop limit. Run Bellman-Ford for `k + 1` rounds instead, updating from a copy of the previous round's costs.

**Input:** The first line has `n` and `m` — the number of nodes (numbered `0` to `n − 1`) and edges. Each of the next `m` lines has an edge `u v p`: a flight from `u` to `v` costing `p`. The last line has `src dst k`.

**Output:** the cheapest price, or `-1`.

examples.explanation: 0 → 1 → 3 costs 700. The cheaper 0 → 1 → 2 → 3 needs two stops.
With no stops only the direct flight works.

title: Bellman-Ford with Negative Cycle Detection
description:
Edge weights in a **directed** graph can be negative. Find the shortest distance from `s` to every node with Bellman-Ford: relax every edge `n − 1` times. If any edge can still be relaxed afterwards, a **negative cycle** is reachable from `s` and shortest paths don't exist.

A negative cycle that `s` can't reach doesn't matter.

**Input:** The first line has `n` and `m` — the number of nodes (numbered `0` to `n − 1`) and edges. Each of the next `m` lines has an edge `u v w` going from `u` to `v` with weight `w`. The last line has the source `s`.

**Output:** `NEGATIVE CYCLE` if a negative cycle is reachable from `s`. Otherwise `n` space-separated distances, using `INF` for unreachable nodes.

examples.explanation: 0 → 2 → 1 costs 2, which beats the direct edge.
1 → 2 → 1 has total weight −2 and is reachable.

title: Floyd-Warshall All Pairs
description:
Find the shortest distance between **every pair** of nodes in a **directed** graph with non-negative weights.

Floyd-Warshall tries each node `k` as a midpoint: `dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j])`, in `O(n³)`.

**Input:** The first line has `n` and `m` — the number of nodes (numbered `0` to `n − 1`) and edges. Each of the next `m` lines has an edge `u v w` going from `u` to `v` with weight `w`.

**Output:** `n` lines with `n` space-separated values each: row `i`, column `j` is the distance from `i` to `j`, `0` when `i = j`, or `-1` if `j` is unreachable from `i`.

examples.explanation: No edges: only the diagonal is reachable.

title: Minimum Spanning Tree Weight
description:
A spanning tree of a connected, **undirected**, weighted graph is a set of `n − 1` edges that connects all nodes. Print the smallest possible total weight of a spanning tree.

Kruskal's algorithm sorts the edges by weight and adds each one that joins two different components (tracked with union-find). Prim's algorithm grows the tree from one node instead.

**Input:** The first line has `n` and `m` — the number of nodes (numbered `0` to `n − 1`) and edges. Each of the next `m` lines has an edge `u v w`. The graph is connected.

**Output:** the total weight of a minimum spanning tree.

examples.explanation: Take 4, 5 and 10 for a total of 19.
A single node needs no edges.

title: Number of Operations to Connect the Network
description:
`n` computers are linked by `m` cables, each joining two computers. In one operation you can unplug any cable and plug it between two other computers.

Print the minimum number of operations needed so that every computer can reach every other, or `-1` if there aren't enough cables (a connected network needs at least `n − 1`).

If there are enough cables, the answer is the number of separate groups minus one: each redundant cable can join two groups.

**Input:** The first line has `n` and `m` — the number of nodes (numbered `0` to `n − 1`) and edges. Each of the next `m` lines has an edge (cable) `u v`.

**Output:** the minimum number of operations, or `-1`.

examples.explanation: Move the redundant cable 1–2 to connect computer 3.

title: Assign Cookies
description:
Each child has a greed value — the smallest cookie size that makes them happy — and each cookie has a size. A child can get at most one cookie and each cookie goes to at most one child. Make as many children happy as possible.

Sort both lists and give the smallest cookie that's big enough to the least greedy child still waiting.

**Input:** line 1 — the children's greed values; line 2 — the cookie sizes.

**Output:** the maximum number of happy children.

examples.explanation: Both cookies are size 1, so only the child with greed 1 is happy.

title: Lemonade Change
description:
Lemonade costs 5. Customers arrive in order and each pays with a 5, 10 or 20 bill. You start with no money. Can you give every customer correct change?

When you have a choice for a 20, give back a 10 + 5 rather than three 5s — 5s are more useful later.

**Input:** one line — the bills in order.

**Output:** `true` if everyone gets correct change, otherwise `false`.

examples.explanation: Keep the 10 from customer 4 and hand it back to customer 5.
The last customer needs 15 but you only hold two 10s.

title: Shortest Job First
description:
A CPU runs jobs one at a time; all jobs arrive at time 0 and each has a burst time. A job's waiting time is how long it waits before it starts. Run the jobs in the order that minimizes the total waiting time (shortest first) and print the **average** waiting time, rounded down to an integer.

**Input:** one line of burst times.

**Output:** `floor(total waiting time / number of jobs)`.

title: Can You Reach the End
description:
You stand on index 0 of an array. The value at each index is the **maximum** number of steps you can jump forward from there. Can you reach the last index?

Track the farthest index reachable so far; if you ever stand beyond it, you're stuck.

**Input:** one line of non-negative integers.

**Output:** `true` or `false`.

examples.explanation: Jump 1 step to index 1, then 3 steps to the end.
Every route lands on the 0 at index 3.

title: Minimum Jumps to the End
description:
Same jumping rules as *Can You Reach the End*, but now the last index is always reachable. Print the minimum number of jumps needed to get there.

Think in levels, like BFS: all indices reachable with `k` jumps form a window; the next window extends to the farthest point reachable from it.

**Input:** one line of non-negative integers.

**Output:** the minimum number of jumps (0 if the array has one element).

title: Maximum Meetings in One Room
description:
There is one meeting room and `n` meetings, each with a start and an end time. Schedule as many meetings as possible. A meeting can only start **strictly after** the previous one ends.

Always pick the meeting that finishes earliest among those that still fit.

**Input:** line 1 — start times; line 2 — end times (same order, `start <= end`).

**Output:** the maximum number of meetings.

examples.explanation: The second starts exactly when the first ends — not allowed.

title: Minimum Platforms
description:
Trains arrive and depart at a station during one day. Times are written as `HHMM` integers (e.g. `905` is 9:05, `1430` is 14:30), and each train departs at or after it arrives. A train occupies a platform from its arrival through its departure, **inclusive** — if one train departs at the same minute another arrives, they need different platforms. Find the minimum number of platforms.

Sort arrivals and departures separately and sweep through both.

**Input:** line 1 — arrival times; line 2 — departure times (same order).

**Output:** the minimum number of platforms.

examples.explanation: Between 11:00 and 11:20 three trains are at the station.

title: Fractional Knapsack
description:
You have a bag of capacity `W` and `n` items, each with a value and a weight. You may take any **fraction** of an item, getting that fraction of its value. Maximize the total value.

Take items in decreasing order of value per unit weight, taking a piece of the last one if it doesn't fully fit.

**Input:** line 1 — `n` and `W`; next `n` lines — `value weight`.

**Output:** the maximum value, rounded to 2 decimal places (half up), e.g. `240.00`.

examples.explanation: Take the first two whole and 2/3 of the third: 60 + 100 + 80.

title: Job Sequencing
description:
Each job takes one unit of time, has a deadline `d` (it must finish by time `d`, i.e. occupy one of the slots 1…d) and a profit. Only one job runs at a time. Choose jobs to maximize the total profit.

Take jobs from most to least profitable and put each in the latest free slot not after its deadline.

**Input:** line 1 — `n`; next `n` lines — `deadline profit`.

**Output:** the maximum total profit.

examples.explanation: Run the 40 job in slot 1 and the 20 job later: 60.

title: Insert an Interval
description:
You're given a list of non-overlapping intervals sorted by start, and one new interval. Insert the new interval and merge wherever intervals overlap. Intervals are closed, so `[1, 2]` and `[2, 3]` overlap and merge into `[1, 3]`.

**Input:** line 1 — `n`; next `n` lines — `start end` of the existing intervals (sorted, disjoint); last line — the new interval `start end`.

**Output:** the resulting intervals in order, one `start end` per line.

title: Non-overlapping Intervals
description:
Remove the fewest intervals so that the remaining ones don't overlap. Intervals that only touch at an endpoint, like `[1, 2]` and `[2, 3]`, do **not** overlap.

Keep the interval that ends earliest; it leaves the most room for the rest.

**Input:** line 1 — `n`; next `n` lines — `start end` with `start < end`.

**Output:** the minimum number of intervals to remove.

title: Gas Station Circuit
description:
Stations sit on a circular road. At station `i` you can fill up `gas[i]` units, and driving from `i` to `i + 1` (wrapping around at the end) costs `cost[i]`. Your tank starts empty and has no limit. From which station can you start and drive the full circle back to it?

If the total gas is less than the total cost, it's impossible. Otherwise, whenever your tank goes negative, no station up to that point can be the start — restart from the next one.

**Input:** line 1 — `gas`; line 2 — `cost`.

**Output:** the **smallest** index you can start from, or `-1` if none works.

examples.explanation: Starting at index 3 you never run dry.
Total gas 9 is less than total cost 10.

title: Wildcard Parentheses
description:
A string contains `(`, `)` and `*`. Each `*` can act as `(`, as `)`, or as nothing. Can the string be made into a balanced parentheses string?

Instead of trying every choice, track the lowest and highest possible number of open brackets as you scan.

**Input:** one string.

**Output:** `true` or `false`.

examples.explanation: The first ) can never be matched.

title: Candy Distribution
description:
Children stand in a line, each with a rating. Give every child at least one candy, and any child with a higher rating than a neighbour must get more candies than that neighbour. What's the fewest candies you need in total?

Do two passes: left to right handles the left neighbour, right to left handles the right one.

**Input:** one line of ratings.

**Output:** the minimum total number of candies.

examples.explanation: Give 1, 2, 1 — equal ratings don't need to differ.

title: Highest and Lowest Frequency Element
description:
Given an array, find the element that appears **most often** and the element that appears **least often** (among the values that appear at all).

If several values share the highest frequency, pick the smallest of them. Do the same for the lowest frequency.

**Input:** one line of space-separated integers.

**Output:** the most frequent value and the least frequent value, separated by a space.

examples.explanation: Both appear twice, so the smallest (2) wins both ties.

title: Isomorphic Strings
description:
Two strings `s` and `t` are **isomorphic** if you can replace every character of `s` to get `t`, where each character always maps to the same character and no two different characters map to the same one. A character may map to itself.

Print `true` if `s` and `t` are isomorphic, otherwise `false`.

**Input:** `s` on the first line, `t` on the second. Both are non-empty lowercase strings.

**Output:** `true` or `false`.

examples.explanation: Both d and b would have to map to b.

title: Distinct Elements in Every Window
description:
Given an array and a window size `k`, count how many **distinct** values are in each contiguous window of `k` elements, from left to right.

Recounting every window is `O(n·k)`. Instead, keep a count map and update it as the window slides: add the entering element, remove the leaving one.

**Input:** the array on the first line, `k` on the second.

**Output:** `n - k + 1` space-separated counts, one per window.

title: Valid Sudoku
description:
You're given a partially filled 9×9 Sudoku board. Decide whether the filled cells are **consistent**: no digit repeats within a row, within a column, or within any of the nine 3×3 boxes.

Empty cells are written as `.`. You don't need to check whether the board can actually be solved, only whether the digits already placed break a rule.

**Input:** 9 lines, each with 9 space-separated tokens (`1`–`9` or `.`).

**Output:** `true` if the board is consistent, otherwise `false`.

examples.explanation: No row, column or box repeats a digit.
The first column has two 8s (and so does the top-left box).

title: Longest Subarray with Sum K
description:
Find the length of the longest contiguous subarray whose elements add up to exactly `k`. The array may contain negative numbers. Print `0` if no subarray has sum `k`.

Keep a running prefix sum and remember the **first** index where each prefix sum appears. If `prefix - k` was seen at index `j`, the subarray after `j` up to here sums to `k`.

**Input:** the array on the first line, `k` on the second.

**Output:** the length of the longest subarray with sum `k`.

title: Count Subarrays with XOR K
description:
Count the contiguous subarrays whose bitwise XOR of all elements equals `k`.

XOR works like a prefix sum: if `P` is the XOR of everything so far, a subarray ending here has XOR `k` exactly when some earlier prefix equals `P ^ k`. Count those prefixes with a hash map.

**Input:** the array of non-negative integers on the first line, `k` on the second.

**Output:** the number of subarrays with XOR equal to `k`.

title: Kth Smallest Element
description:
Print the `k`-th smallest value in the array (counting duplicates, so `k = 1` is the minimum).

Sorting works in `O(n log n)`. A max-heap holding only the `k` smallest values seen so far does it in `O(n log k)`: push each value and pop the largest whenever the heap grows past `k`.

**Input:** the first line is the array; the second line is `k`.

**Output:** the `k`-th smallest value.

examples.explanation: Duplicates count: 1 5 5, so the second is 5.

title: Last Stone Weight
description:
You have a pile of stones with positive weights. Each turn, take the two heaviest stones `x ≥ y` and smash them: if they're equal both are destroyed, otherwise a stone of weight `x − y` goes back on the pile. Stop when at most one stone is left.

A max-heap gives you the two heaviest stones in `O(log n)` per turn.

**Input:** one line of space-separated stone weights.

**Output:** the weight of the last stone, or `0` if none remain.

examples.explanation: 8 and 7 → 1, 4 and 2 → 2, 2 and 1 → 1, 1 and 1 → gone, leaving 1.

title: Minimum Cost to Connect Ropes
description:
You have ropes of the given lengths. Joining two ropes of lengths `a` and `b` costs `a + b` and produces one rope of that length. Join all ropes into one with the **minimum total cost**.

Greedy works: always join the two shortest ropes, using a min-heap.

**Input:** one line of space-separated rope lengths.

**Output:** the minimum total cost (`0` if there is only one rope).

title: Kth Largest in a Stream
description:
Numbers arrive one at a time. After each new number, report the `k`-th largest number seen so far (duplicates count). If fewer than `k` numbers have arrived, report `-1`.

Keep a min-heap of the `k` largest values: its top is the answer.

**Input:** the first line is `k`, the second is `q`, then `q` lines of the form `add x`.

**Output:** one line per `add`: the current `k`-th largest, or `-1`.

examples.explanation: Fewer than 3 numbers at first, then 4, 4, 5.
With k = 1 it's the running maximum.

A min-heap of size `k + 1` always contains the next smallest element, which gives `O(n log k)` — faster than a full sort when `k` is small.

**Input:** the first line is the array; the second line is `k`.

**Output:** the sorted array, space-separated.

examples.explanation: Each value is within 3 places of its sorted spot.

title: Merge K Sorted Arrays
description:
You're given `k` arrays, each sorted in non-decreasing order. Merge them into one sorted array.

Put the first element of each array into a min-heap along with which array it came from. Repeatedly pop the smallest and push the next element from the same array: `O(N log k)` for `N` total elements.

**Input:** the first line is `k`, followed by `k` lines, each a sorted, non-empty list of integers.

**Output:** all values in sorted order, space-separated.

examples.explanation: Taking the smallest front each time gives 1 through 9.

title: Top K Frequent Elements
description:
Print the `k` values that appear most often. Order them from most to least frequent; when two values appear equally often, the **smaller value comes first** (and wins a spot if they tie at the cut-off).

Count with a hash map, then take the top `k` with a heap (or bucket sort by frequency).

**Input:** the first line is the array; the second line is `k` (at most the number of distinct values).

**Output:** the `k` values, space-separated, in the order described.

examples.explanation: 4 and 5 tie at two each; the smaller, 4, wins.

title: K Closest Points to Origin
description:
Given points on a plane, print the `k` points closest to the origin `(0, 0)` by Euclidean distance.

Order the output by distance (closest first). Break ties by smaller `x`, then smaller `y`. Compare squared distances `x² + y²` to stay in integers.

**Input:** the first line has `n` and `k`, followed by `n` lines with a point `x y`.

**Output:** `k` lines, each a point `x y`, in the order described.

examples.explanation: Squared distances 18, 26, 20: the closest two are (3, 3) then (-2, 4).
Both at distance 1 — the smaller x, 0, comes first.

title: Hand of Straights
description:
Can the cards be split into groups of exactly `g` cards each, where every group is `g` **consecutive** values (like 3, 4, 5)? Every card must be used.

Greedy: the smallest remaining card must start a group, so repeatedly take the smallest value and consume one card of each value up to `smallest + g − 1`.

**Input:** the first line is the card values; the second line is `g`.

**Output:** `true` or `false`.

title: Task Scheduler
description:
A CPU runs tasks labelled by capital letters, one per time unit. Two runs of the **same** task must be separated by at least `n` units, during which the CPU can run other tasks or sit idle. Tasks can run in any order. Print the minimum number of time units to finish everything.

The most frequent task decides the shape: with maximum count `m` and `t` tasks sharing that count, the answer is `max(total, (m − 1)·(n + 1) + t)`. You can also simulate it with a max-heap.

**Input:** the first line is the task letters, space-separated; the second line is `n`.

**Output:** the minimum number of time units.

A A A B B B
2

title: Find Median from Data Stream
description:
Process a stream of operations: `add x` adds a number, and `median` asks for the median of all numbers added so far. With an even count, the median is the average of the two middle values.

Keep two heaps: a max-heap for the smaller half and a min-heap for the larger half, rebalanced so their sizes differ by at most one. Each operation is `O(log n)`.

**Input:** the first line is `q`, followed by `q` operations. The first operation is always `add`.

**Output:** one line per `median`, printed with exactly one decimal place (e.g. `2.0`, `2.5`, `-1.5`).
