title: Linked List Length
description:
Count the nodes of a linked list by walking it from the head until you fall off the end.

A linked list is written on one line as its node values from head to tail, space-separated. An empty list is written as `null`.

**Input:** one line, the list.

**Output:** the number of nodes.

examples.explanation: An empty list has no nodes.

title: Insert Node at Position
description:
Insert a new node with value `val` so that it ends up at 0-based position `pos`. Position 0 makes it the new head; position `n` (the length) appends it at the tail.

A linked list is written on one line as its node values from head to tail, space-separated. An empty list is written as `null`.

**Input:** line 1 is the list; line 2 has `pos` and `val`.

**Output:** the list after the insertion.

examples.explanation: Inserting into an empty list creates a single node.

title: Delete Node with Value
description:
Remove the **first** node whose value equals `x`. If no node has that value, the list is unchanged.

A linked list is written on one line as its node values from head to tail, space-separated. An empty list is written as `null`.

**Input:** line 1 is the list; line 2 is `x`.

**Output:** the list after the deletion (`null` if it becomes empty).

examples.explanation: Deleting the only node leaves an empty list.

title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted List
description:
The list is sorted in non-decreasing order. Remove nodes so that every value appears exactly once, keeping the list sorted.

Because equal values sit next to each other, one pass that skips a node whenever it equals its predecessor is enough.

A linked list is written on one line as its node values from head to tail, space-separated. An empty list is written as `null`.

**Input:** one line, the sorted list.

**Output:** the list with duplicates removed.

title: Palindrome Linked List
description:
Print `true` if the list reads the same forwards and backwards, otherwise `false`.

Try to do it with `O(1)` extra space: find the middle with slow/fast pointers, reverse the second half, then compare the halves.

A linked list is written on one line as its node values from head to tail, space-separated. An empty list is written as `null`.

**Input:** one line, the list.

**Output:** `true` or `false`.

title: Delete the Middle Node
description:
Delete the middle node of the list. For a list of length `n`, the middle is the node at 0-based index `⌊n / 2⌋`, so in a list of 4 nodes the third node is removed.

Do it in one pass: a fast pointer moving two steps per slow step stops when the slow pointer is just before the middle.

A linked list is written on one line as its node values from head to tail, space-separated. An empty list is written as `null`.

**Input:** one line, the list.

**Output:** the list without its middle node (`null` if it becomes empty).

title: Odd Even Linked List
description:
Regroup the list so that all nodes at odd positions (1st, 3rd, 5th, …) come first, followed by all nodes at even positions. Keep the relative order inside each group. Positions are about where a node sits, not its value.

A linked list is written on one line as its node values from head to tail, space-separated. An empty list is written as `null`.

**Input:** one line, the list.

**Output:** the regrouped list.

title: Sort a 0-1-2 Linked List
description:
Every node holds 0, 1 or 2. Rearrange the nodes so all 0s come first, then 1s, then 2s.

Instead of counting and overwriting values, try relinking the nodes into three separate chains and joining them.

A linked list is written on one line as its node values from head to tail, space-separated. An empty list is written as `null`.

**Input:** one line, the list.

**Output:** the sorted list.

title: Swap Nodes in Pairs
description:
Swap every two adjacent nodes: the 1st with the 2nd, the 3rd with the 4th, and so on. If the length is odd, the last node stays where it is. Move the nodes themselves rather than swapping their values.

A linked list is written on one line as its node values from head to tail, space-separated. An empty list is written as `null`.

**Input:** one line, the list.

**Output:** the list after swapping pairs.

title: Add Two Numbers
description:
Two non-negative integers are stored as linked lists of digits in **reverse order**: the head holds the ones digit. Add them and print the sum in the same reversed-digit form.

Neither number has leading zeros, except the number 0 itself (a single node `0`). The numbers can be much longer than any built-in integer type, so add digit by digit with a carry.

**Input:** two lines, each a list of digits (space-separated, ones digit first).

**Output:** the digits of the sum, space-separated, ones digit first.

title: Rotate List
description:
Rotate the list to the right by `k` places: each step moves the tail node to the front. `k` may be larger than the list's length.

Connect the tail to the head to form a ring, then cut it at the right place: `k mod n` nodes from the end.

A linked list is written on one line as its node values from head to tail, space-separated. An empty list is written as `null`.

**Input:** line 1 is the list; line 2 is `k`.

**Output:** the rotated list.

title: Reverse Sublist Between Positions
description:
Reverse only the part of the list from position `left` to position `right` (1-based, inclusive), leaving the rest in place. Try to do it in a single pass.

A linked list is written on one line as its node values from head to tail, space-separated. An empty list is written as `null`.

**Input:** line 1 is a non-empty list; line 2 has `left` and `right`.

**Output:** the list after reversing that section.

examples.explanation: A one-node section doesn't change anything.

title: Partition List
description:
Rearrange the list so that every node with a value **less than** `x` comes before every node with a value greater than or equal to `x`. Keep the original relative order within both parts.

A linked list is written on one line as its node values from head to tail, space-separated. An empty list is written as `null`.

**Input:** line 1 is the list; line 2 is `x`.

**Output:** the partitioned list.

examples.explanation: Values below 3 (1 2 2) keep their order, then 4 3 5.

title: Sort Linked List
description:
Sort the list in non-decreasing order. Aim for `O(n log n)` time: split the list at its middle, sort both halves recursively, and merge them (merge sort suits linked lists well because merging needs no extra array).

A linked list is written on one line as its node values from head to tail, space-separated. An empty list is written as `null`.

**Input:** one line, the list.

**Output:** the sorted list.

title: Reverse Nodes in k-Group
description:
Reverse the nodes of the list `k` at a time. Each full group of `k` consecutive nodes is reversed; if fewer than `k` nodes remain at the end, they stay in their original order.

A linked list is written on one line as its node values from head to tail, space-separated. An empty list is written as `null`.

**Input:** line 1 is a non-empty list; line 2 is `k`.

**Output:** the list after reversing every full group.

examples.explanation: (1 2) and (3 4) are reversed; 5 is left alone.

title: Merge K Sorted Lists
description:
You are given `k` linked lists, each sorted in non-decreasing order. Merge them into one sorted list.

A min-heap holding the current head of every list gives `O(N log k)` for `N` total nodes.

A linked list is written on one line as its node values from head to tail, space-separated. An empty list is written as `null`.

**Input:** line 1 is `k`; each of the next `k` lines is one sorted list (possibly `null`).

**Output:** the merged list (`null` if every list is empty).

examples.explanation: One empty list and one single node.

title: Binary Strings Without Consecutive Ones
description:
Print every binary string of length `n` that never has two `1`s next to each other.

Build the string one character at a time: you can always append `0`, but you may append `1` only when the last character isn't `1`.

**Input:** one integer `n`.

**Output:** the valid strings, one per line, in lexicographic (dictionary) order.

examples.explanation: Of the 8 strings of length 3, five avoid "11".

title: Generate Parentheses
description:
Print every string of `n` pairs of parentheses that is correctly balanced.

Add `(` while you still have opening brackets left, and add `)` only when it closes an open one — that way every string you build stays valid.

**Input:** one integer `n`.

**Output:** all balanced strings, one per line, in lexicographic order (`(` comes before `)`).

examples.explanation: There are 5 balanced strings with 3 pairs.

title: Subsets (Power Set)
description:
Given an array of **distinct** integers, print every subset (the power set).

For each element you have two choices — take it or leave it — so there are `2^n` subsets.

**Input:** one line of space-separated distinct integers.

**Output:** one subset per line as `[a b c]` with its elements in increasing order (the empty subset is `[]`). Order the lines by comparing subsets element by element, where a shorter prefix comes first — e.g. `[]`, `[1]`, `[1 2]`, `[1 2 3]`, `[1 3]`, `[2]`, …

title: Subset Sums
description:
For an array of `n` integers, compute the sum of every one of its `2^n` subsets (including the empty subset, whose sum is 0).

**Input:** one line of space-separated integers.

**Output:** all `2^n` sums, space-separated, in non-decreasing order. Equal sums from different subsets are all printed.

title: Subsets With Duplicates
description:
The array may contain repeated values. Print every **distinct** subset — two subsets count as the same if they contain the same values the same number of times.

Sort first, then while choosing the next element at a given depth, skip a value equal to the one you just tried.

**Input:** one line of space-separated integers.

**Output:** one subset per line as `[a b c]` with elements in increasing order (`[]` for empty), lines ordered as in *Subsets (Power Set)*: compare element by element, shorter prefix first.

examples.explanation: [2] and [1 2] appear once each even though there are two 2s.

title: Combination Sum
description:
Given a list of distinct positive candidate numbers and a `target`, print every combination of candidates that adds up to `target`. **Each candidate may be used any number of times.**

**Input:** line 1 — the candidates; line 2 — `target`.

**Output:** one combination per line as `[a b c]` with values in non-decreasing order, lines sorted by comparing element by element (shorter prefix first). Print `none` if there is no combination.

title: Combination Sum II
description:
Given candidate numbers (possibly with repeats) and a `target`, print every combination that sums to `target` where **each array element is used at most once**. Don't print the same combination twice.

**Input:** line 1 — the candidates; line 2 — `target`.

**Output:** one combination per line as `[a b c]` in non-decreasing order, lines sorted by comparing element by element (shorter prefix first). Print `none` if there is no combination.

examples.explanation: The two 1s can be used together in [1 1 6].

title: Combination Sum III
description:
Find every set of exactly `k` **different** digits from 1 to 9 whose sum is `n`.

**Input:** one line with `k` and `n`.

**Output:** one combination per line as `[a b c]` in increasing order, lines sorted lexicographically by their numbers. Print `none` if no combination exists.

examples.explanation: Four different digits sum to at least 10.

title: Permutations
description:
Print every ordering (permutation) of an array of **distinct** integers.

**Input:** one line of space-separated distinct integers.

**Output:** one permutation per line, values space-separated, lines in lexicographic order of the numbers.

title: Letter Combinations of a Phone Number
description:
On a phone keypad, 2 → `abc`, 3 → `def`, 4 → `ghi`, 5 → `jkl`, 6 → `mno`, 7 → `pqrs`, 8 → `tuv`, 9 → `wxyz`. Given a string of digits from 2 to 9, print every letter string it could spell.

**Input:** one line of digits (2–9).

**Output:** all possible strings, one per line, in lexicographic order.

examples.output:
ad
ae
af
bd
be
bf
cd
ce
cf

title: N-Queens
description:
Place `n` queens on an `n × n` chessboard so that no two attack each other (no shared row, column or diagonal).

**Input:** one integer `n`.

**Output:** line 1 — the number of valid placements. If there is at least one, then print the board of the **first** placement in this order: compare placements row by row by the column of that row's queen, smallest first. Print the board as `n` lines using `Q` for a queen and `.` for an empty square.

examples.explanation: Two placements; the first has queens in columns 1, 3, 0, 2.

title: Graph M-Coloring
description:
Can the vertices of an undirected graph be colored with at most `k` colors so that no edge connects two vertices of the same color?

**Input:** line 1 — `n` (vertices numbered 0…n−1), `m` (edges) and `k`; next `m` lines — edges `u v`.

**Output:** `true` if such a coloring exists, otherwise `false`.

examples.explanation: Color 0 and 2 differently from everything around them.

title: Sudoku Solver
description:
Solve a 9 × 9 Sudoku: fill the empty cells so that every row, every column and every 3 × 3 box contains each digit 1–9 exactly once. Every puzzle given has exactly one solution.

**Input:** 9 lines of 9 characters each; `0` marks an empty cell.

**Output:** the solved grid as 9 lines of 9 digits.
constraints: The puzzle has exactly one solution.

examples.explanation: Try digits in empty cells, backing up when a row, column or box conflicts.

title: Maximum Sum Subarray of Size K
description:
Find the largest sum of any `k` consecutive elements.

Compute the first window's sum, then slide: add the element entering on the right and subtract the one leaving on the left. Each step is `O(1)`.

**Input:** line 1 is the array; line 2 is `k`.

**Output:** the maximum window sum.

examples.explanation: With negatives only, pick the largest single value.

title: Maximum Points from Cards
description:
Cards lie in a row, each worth some points. You must take exactly `k` cards, and each time you may only take a card from the **left end or the right end** of the row. Maximise your total.

Any valid choice takes some cards from the left and the rest from the right. Start with all `k` from the left, then trade them one at a time for cards from the right.

**Input:** line 1 is the card values; line 2 is `k`.

**Output:** the maximum total.

examples.explanation: Taking all three from the right (5 + 6 + 1 = 12) beats any mix with the left end.

title: Max Consecutive Ones III
description:
The array holds only `0`s and `1`s. You may flip at most `k` zeros into ones. Print the length of the longest run of consecutive ones you can get.

Equivalently: find the longest window that contains at most `k` zeros.

**Input:** line 1 is the array; line 2 is `k`.

**Output:** the longest possible run.

examples.explanation: Flip the two zeros before the run of four ones: length 6.
No flips allowed and no ones.

title: Minimum Size Subarray Sum
description:
All values are positive. Find the length of the shortest contiguous subarray whose sum is **at least** `target`. Print `0` if no such subarray exists.

Because every value is positive, growing the window only increases the sum and shrinking it only decreases it, so two pointers work.

**Input:** line 1 is the array; line 2 is `target`.

**Output:** the minimal length, or `0`.

examples.explanation: The whole array only sums to 3.

title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
description:
The string contains uppercase letters. You may change at most `k` characters to any other uppercase letter. Print the length of the longest substring that consists of a single repeated letter after the changes.

A window is fixable when `window length − (count of its most frequent letter) <= k`.

**Input:** line 1 is the string; line 2 is `k`.

**Output:** the longest achievable length.

examples.explanation: Change both A's (or both B's): length 4.
Change the A in BABB to get BBBB, length 4.

title: Subarray Product Less Than K
description:
All values are positive. Count the contiguous subarrays whose product is **strictly less** than `k`.

When the window `[left, right]` is valid, every subarray ending at `right` and starting at or after `left` is valid too, adding `right − left + 1` to the count.

**Input:** line 1 is the array; line 2 is `k`.

**Output:** the number of such subarrays.

title: Binary Subarrays With Sum
description:
The array holds only `0`s and `1`s. Count the contiguous subarrays whose sum equals exactly `goal`.

"Exactly `goal`" is hard to slide directly, but "at most `goal`" is easy. Use `count(sum <= goal) − count(sum <= goal − 1)`.

**Input:** line 1 is the array; line 2 is `goal`.

**Output:** the number of subarrays.

examples.explanation: Four subarrays contain exactly two ones.

title: Subarrays with K Different Integers
description:
Count the contiguous subarrays that contain **exactly** `k` distinct integers.

As with sums, "exactly `k`" equals "at most `k`" minus "at most `k − 1`", and "at most `k` distinct" is a standard sliding window with a frequency map.

**Input:** line 1 is the array; line 2 is `k`.

**Output:** the number of subarrays.

title: Minimum Window Substring
description:
Find the shortest substring of `s` that contains every character of `t`, counting repeats (if `t` has two `a`s, the window needs at least two `a`s). Characters are case-sensitive.

If several shortest windows exist, print the **leftmost** one. If no window works, print `-1`.

**Input:** line 1 is `s`; line 2 is `t`. Both contain only English letters.

**Output:** the minimum window, or `-1`.

examples.explanation: BANC is the shortest window holding A, B and C.

title: Check if Array Is Sorted
description:
Print `true` if the array is sorted in non-decreasing order (each element is at most the next one), otherwise `false`. Equal neighbours are allowed.

**Input:** one line of space-separated integers.

**Output:** `true` or `false`.

title: Insertion Sort
description:
Sort the array in non-decreasing order **by implementing insertion sort yourself** (don't call a built-in sort — the point is the algorithm).

Insertion sort grows a sorted prefix one element at a time: take the next element and shift larger elements of the prefix one step right until its slot opens up. It's `O(n²)` in general but very fast on nearly-sorted input.

**Input:** one line of space-separated integers.

**Output:** the sorted integers, space-separated.

examples.explanation: Insert 11 before 12, keep 13, then slide 5 and 6 into place.

title: Counting Sort
description:
All values are small (between 0 and 1000), so you can sort without comparing elements: count how many times each value appears, then write each value out that many times. This runs in `O(n + k)` where `k` is the value range.

**Input:** one line of space-separated integers, each between 0 and 1000.

**Output:** the sorted integers, space-separated.

title: Sort Array by Parity
description:
Rearrange the array so that every even number comes before every odd number. Keep the **original relative order** within the evens and within the odds (a stable partition).

**Input:** one line of space-separated integers.

**Output:** the rearranged integers, space-separated.

examples.explanation: Evens 2, 4 keep their order, then odds 3, 1.

title: Sort 0s 1s and 2s
description:
The array contains only 0s, 1s and 2s. Sort it in a **single pass** with constant extra space.

Keep three regions with pointers `low`, `mid` and `high`: everything before `low` is 0, between `low` and `mid` is 1, after `high` is 2. Look at `a[mid]` and swap it into the right region (the Dutch national flag algorithm).

**Input:** one line of space-separated values, each 0, 1 or 2.

**Output:** the sorted values, space-separated.

title: Sort by Frequency
description:
Sort the array so that values that appear **more often come first**. If two values appear the same number of times, the **smaller value comes first**. Equal values stay grouped together.

**Input:** one line of space-separated integers.

**Output:** the reordered integers, space-separated.

examples.explanation: All appear once, so order by value.

title: Queue Using Two Stacks
description:
Build a first-in, first-out queue using only two stacks. Push onto an *inbox* stack; when you need the front, pour the inbox into an *outbox* stack, which reverses the order. Each element moves at most twice, so every operation is `O(1)` amortised.

Commands:
- `push x`: add `x` to the back.
- `pop`: remove and print the front element, or `-1` if the queue is empty.
- `peek`: print the front element without removing it, or `-1` if empty.
- `empty`: print `true` if the queue is empty, otherwise `false`.

**Input:** line 1 is `q`; each of the next `q` lines is one command.

**Output:** one line for every `pop`, `peek` and `empty` command, in order.

examples.explanation: 1 is at the front; after popping it, 2 remains.

title: Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation
description:
Evaluate an expression written in reverse Polish (postfix) notation, where each operator follows its two operands. For example `2 1 + 3 *` means `(2 + 1) × 3`.

Operators are `+`, `-`, `*` and `/`. Division between integers **truncates toward zero** (`7 / -3 = -2`). The expression is always valid and never divides by zero.

**Input:** one line of space-separated tokens.

**Output:** the value of the expression.

title: Infix to Postfix
description:
Convert an infix expression to postfix (reverse Polish) notation.

Operands are single lowercase letters. Operators, from lowest to highest precedence: `+ -`, then `* /`, then `^`. `+ - * /` are left-associative; `^` is **right-associative** (`a^b^c` means `a^(b^c)`). Parentheses group as usual and do not appear in the output.

**Input:** one line, the expression (no spaces).

**Output:** the postfix expression, with no spaces.

examples.explanation: * binds tighter, so b c * comes first: abc*+.
Parentheses first; ^ groups from the right.

title: Next Smaller Element
description:
For every element, find the first element to its **right** that is strictly smaller. Print `-1` if there is none.

Scan from right to left with a stack that stays increasing from bottom to top: pop everything that is not smaller than the current element, and whatever is left on top is the answer.

**Input:** one line of space-separated integers.

**Output:** the answers, space-separated, in the original order.

examples.explanation: Equal values don't count as smaller.

title: Next Greater Element II
description:
The array is **circular**: after the last element comes the first one again. For every element, find the first strictly greater element you meet when walking forward (wrapping around). Print `-1` if there is none.

Iterate over the array twice (indices `2n − 1` down to 0) with a decreasing stack, so the wrap-around is handled without copying.

**Input:** one line of space-separated integers.

**Output:** the answers, space-separated, in the original order.

examples.explanation: The last 1 wraps around to find 2; 2 has nothing greater.

title: Daily Temperatures
description:
Given daily temperatures, print for each day how many days you have to wait for a strictly warmer day. If no warmer day comes, print `0` for that day.

**Input:** one line of space-separated temperatures.

**Output:** the waits, space-separated.

examples.explanation: Day 0 waits 1 day for 74; day 2 waits 4 days for 76.
Each day is warmed by the next.

title: Stock Span
description:
The **span** of a stock's price on a day is the number of consecutive days, ending with that day and counting backwards, on which the price was less than or equal to that day's price. Print the span for every day.

**Input:** one line of space-separated prices.

**Output:** the spans, space-separated.

examples.explanation: On the 75 day the run 60 70 60 75 gives span 4.

title: Asteroid Collision
description:
Asteroids move along a line. The absolute value is the size; a positive sign means it moves right, negative means it moves left. All move at the same speed.

When a right-mover meets a left-mover, the smaller one explodes; if they are the same size, both explode. Two asteroids moving the same way never meet. Print the asteroids that remain after all collisions, left to right, or `empty` if none remain.

**Input:** one line of space-separated non-zero integers.

**Output:** the surviving asteroids, space-separated, or `empty`.

title: Remove K Digits
description:
Given a non-negative integer as a string, remove exactly `k` digits so the number that remains is as small as possible. Print it without leading zeros; if nothing (or only zeros) is left, print `0`.

Greedy idea: walking left to right, whenever the previous kept digit is larger than the current one, removing it makes the number smaller.

**Input:** line 1 is the number (no leading zeros unless it is `0`); line 2 is `k`.

**Output:** the smallest possible result.

examples.explanation: Remove the 1; leading zeros vanish, leaving 200.

title: Sum of Subarray Minimums
description:
For every contiguous subarray, take its minimum. Print the sum of all those minimums modulo `1000000007`.

Instead of listing subarrays, count for each element how many subarrays it is the minimum of: (distance to the previous smaller element) × (distance to the next smaller-or-equal element). Breaking ties on one side only stops subarrays from being counted twice.

**Input:** one line of space-separated positive integers.

**Output:** the sum modulo 1000000007.

title: LRU Cache
description:
Simulate a **least recently used** cache with a fixed capacity.

- `get k`: print the value stored for key `k`, or `-1` if it isn't cached. A successful get makes `k` the most recently used key.
- `put k v`: store `v` under `k` (updating it if present) and make `k` the most recently used key. If this pushes the size over the capacity, evict the least recently used key.

Both operations should be `O(1)`: pair a hash map with a doubly linked list ordered by recency.

**Input:** line 1 has `capacity` and `q`; each of the next `q` lines is a command.

**Output:** one line per `get` command. If there are no `get` commands, print `none`.

examples.input:
2 6
put 1 1
put 2 2
get 1
put 3 3
get 2
get 3
examples.explanation: get 1 refreshes key 1, so putting 3 evicts key 2.

title: Sliding Window Maximum
description:
A window of size `k` slides from the left end of the array to the right end, one step at a time. Print the maximum of every window position.

Keep a deque of indices whose values are decreasing: the front is always the current maximum, and an index leaves from the front once it slides out of the window. That's `O(n)` overall.

**Input:** line 1 is the array; line 2 is `k`.

**Output:** the `n − k + 1` window maximums, space-separated.

examples.explanation: Window size 1 just repeats the array.

title: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
description:
Bars of width 1 stand side by side with the given heights. Find the area of the largest rectangle that fits entirely inside the histogram.

For each bar, the widest rectangle using its full height stretches until a shorter bar on each side. A stack of increasing heights finds those boundaries in one pass.

**Input:** one line of space-separated non-negative heights.

**Output:** the largest area.

examples.explanation: The single bar of height 4 gives 4.

title: Maximal Rectangle
description:
Given a grid of `0`s and `1`s, find the area of the largest rectangle containing only `1`s.

Treat each row as the floor of a histogram: the height in a column is the number of consecutive `1`s ending at that row. Run the largest-rectangle-in-histogram algorithm on every row.

**Input:** line 1 has `r` and `c`; each of the next `r` lines is a string of `c` characters, each `0` or `1`.

**Output:** the largest all-ones rectangle area.

examples.explanation: The 2 × 3 block of ones in rows 2–3 gives 6.

title: Largest Odd Number in String
description:
The string `num` holds the digits of a large non-negative integer. Find the largest-valued **odd** integer that is a non-empty contiguous substring of `num`, and print it exactly as it appears. If there is no odd substring, print `none`.

Hint: a number is odd when its last digit is odd, and keeping more of the prefix only makes it bigger.

**Input:** one line with `num` (digits only, no leading zeros unless it is `0`).

**Output:** the largest odd substring, or `none`.

examples.explanation: The whole number ends in 7, which is odd.

title: Remove Outermost Parentheses
description:
A balanced parentheses string can be split into **primitive** parts: non-empty balanced pieces that can't be split any further. For example `(()())(())` splits into `(()())` and `(())`.

Remove the outermost pair of parentheses from every primitive part and print what's left. If nothing is left, print `none`.

Track the current depth: copy a character only when it isn't the opening or closing bracket at depth zero.

**Input:** one line with a balanced string of `(` and `)`.

**Output:** the string after removing each part's outer parentheses, or `none`.

examples.explanation: Each part is just (), which leaves nothing.

title: Reverse Words in a String
description:
Reverse the order of the words in a line. A word is a run of non-space characters. Words may be separated by more than one space; print them separated by exactly **one** space.

**Input:** one line of words.

**Output:** the words in reverse order, separated by single spaces.
constraints: s contains at least one word

examples.explanation: Read the words from the end.
Extra spaces between words collapse to one.

title: Rotate String Check
description:
A **rotation** moves some characters from the front of a string to its back, so `abcde` can become `cdeab`. Rotating by zero is allowed. Print `true` if `goal` is a rotation of `s`, otherwise `false`.

Neat trick: every rotation of `s` appears inside `s + s`.

**Input:** `s` on the first line, `goal` on the second.

**Output:** `true` or `false`.

examples.explanation: No rotation swaps the last two letters.

title: Maximum Nesting Depth of Parentheses
description:
You're given a valid expression made of digits, the operators `+ - * /` and parentheses. Its **nesting depth** is the largest number of parentheses that are open at the same time. Print the nesting depth (0 if there are no parentheses).

**Input:** one line with the expression.

**Output:** the maximum nesting depth.

examples.explanation: The 8 sits inside three open parentheses.

title: Roman to Integer
description:
Convert a Roman numeral to an integer. The symbols are `I = 1`, `V = 5`, `X = 10`, `L = 50`, `C = 100`, `D = 500` and `M = 1000`. Symbols are normally written largest to smallest and added up, but a smaller symbol placed **before** a larger one is subtracted: `IV = 4`, `IX = 9`, `XL = 40`, `XC = 90`, `CD = 400`, `CM = 900`.

**Input:** one line with a valid Roman numeral.

**Output:** its value.

title: Integer to Roman
description:
Convert an integer to its standard Roman numeral, using the symbols `I V X L C D M` and the subtractive pairs `IV IX XL XC CD CM`. Always use the shortest standard form (so 4 is `IV`, never `IIII`).

Go through the values from largest to smallest (including the six subtractive pairs) and take each one as many times as it fits.

**Input:** one integer `n`.

**Output:** `n` as a Roman numeral.

title: Sort Characters by Frequency
description:
Rearrange the characters of a string so that more frequent characters come first, with all copies of the same character kept together. When two characters appear equally often, the one with the smaller character code (`ASCII` order) comes first.

**Input:** one line with the string (letters and digits, no spaces).

**Output:** the rearranged string.

examples.explanation: e appears twice; r and t once each, r first.
b twice, then A before a (uppercase sorts first).

title: String to Integer
description:
Parse an integer out of a line of text, following these rules exactly:

1. Skip any leading spaces.
2. An optional `+` or `-` sign may come next.
3. Read digits until the first non-digit character or the end of the line. Everything after that is ignored.
4. If no digits were read, the result is `0`.
5. Clamp the result to the 32-bit signed range `[-2147483648, 2147483647]`.

**Input:** one line of text.

**Output:** the parsed integer.
constraints: s contains letters, digits, spaces, '+', '-' and '.'

examples.explanation: Reading stops at the space after 4193.

title: Count Palindromic Substrings
description:
Count the substrings of `s` that read the same forwards and backwards. Substrings at different positions count separately, even if they're equal.

Every palindrome has a center: a single character (odd length) or the gap between two characters (even length). Expand outward from all `2n - 1` centers for `O(n²)` without extra memory.

**Input:** one line with a lowercase string.

**Output:** the number of palindromic substrings.

examples.explanation: a, a, a, aa, aa and aaa.

title: Sum of Beauty of All Substrings
description:
The **beauty** of a string is the frequency of its most common character minus the frequency of its least common character (counting only characters that appear). For example, `aabcb` has beauty `2 - 1 = 1`.

Print the sum of the beauty of every substring of `s`.

Fix each start position and extend the end one character at a time, updating a 26-slot frequency table as you go.

**Input:** one line with a lowercase string.

**Output:** the total beauty.

examples.explanation: Substrings with non-zero beauty: aab, aabc, aabcb, abcb, bcb, each with beauty 1.
One distinct letter means beauty 0 everywhere.

title: Postorder Traversal
description:
Print the values of a binary tree in **postorder**: left subtree, then right subtree, then the node itself.

**Input:** a binary tree as space-separated level-order values, with `null` for a missing child (an empty tree is just `null`).

**Output:** the postorder values space-separated, or `empty` if the tree has no nodes.

examples.explanation: Children 4 and 5 come before 2, both subtrees before the root 1.
3 is the left child of 2, so the order is 3, 2, 1.

title: Boundary Traversal
description:
Print the boundary of a binary tree going anticlockwise, starting from the root. The boundary is made of four parts, with no node printed twice:

1. **The root.**
2. **The left boundary**, top-down: start at the root's left child, and at each step move to the left child if there is one, otherwise the right child. Leaves are left out (they come in part 3). If the root has no left child, this part is empty.
3. **All leaves** from left to right (excluding the root).
4. **The right boundary**, bottom-up: start at the root's right child and move to the right child if there is one, otherwise the left child, leaving out leaves; print these nodes in reverse (bottom to top). If the root has no right child, this part is empty.

A tree that is just a root prints only the root.

**Input:** a binary tree as space-separated level-order values, with `null` for a missing child (an empty tree is just `null`).

**Output:** the boundary values space-separated, or `empty` for an empty tree.

title: Trie With Counts and Erase
description:
Build a trie that stores words **with multiplicity** and supports:

- `insert w` — add one copy of `w`.
- `countEqual w` — how many copies of exactly `w` are stored?
- `countPrefix p` — how many stored words (counting copies) start with `p`?
- `erase w` — remove one copy of `w`; if `w` isn't stored, do nothing.

Keep two counters per node: how many words pass through it and how many end at it.

**Input:** line 1 — `q`; next `q` lines — one command each.

**Output:** one line per `countEqual` / `countPrefix` command with the count.

examples.input:
7
insert apple
insert apple
insert apps
countEqual apple
countPrefix app
erase apple
countPrefix app
examples.explanation: Two apples and one apps, then one apple is erased.
Erasing a missing word does nothing.

title: Count Distinct Substrings
description:
Count how many **different** non-empty substrings a string has.

Insert every suffix into a trie: each new node created is a substring you haven't seen before.

**Input:** one lowercase string `s`.

**Output:** the number of distinct non-empty substrings.

examples.explanation: a, b, ab, ba, aba, bab, abab — 7.

title: Maximum XOR of Two Numbers
description:
Find the largest value of `nums[i] XOR nums[j]` over all pairs (`i` and `j` may be equal, so a single-element array gives 0).

Put every number's 31-bit binary form into a trie. For each number, walk the trie preferring the opposite bit at every level — that greedily maximizes the XOR from the top bit down.

**Input:** one line of non-negative integers.

**Output:** the maximum XOR.

title: Maximum XOR With a Limit
description:
You get an array `nums` and queries `(x, m)`. For each query, find the maximum of `x XOR a` over all `a` in `nums` with `a <= m`. If no element is `<= m`, the answer is `-1`.

Answer queries offline: sort them by `m`, sort `nums`, and add elements to a bitwise trie only once they're allowed.

**Input:** line 1 — `nums`; line 2 — `q`; next `q` lines — `x m`.

**Output:** one answer per query, in the original query order.

examples.explanation: Nothing is ≤ 1 in the second query.
